newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Ciller regains temporary hold on top job.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Ciller regains temporary hold on top job.

text.p: Tansu Ciller, Turkey's first woman leader, is set to regain a temporary grip on the top government post.
But the collapse of her alliance with the Islamists has left her facing her greatest-ever challenge as she tries to salvage her political career.

Ciller, the deputy prime minister, told a news conference on Sunday she would lead a caretaker government from the end of June until early elections aimed at ending a crisis sparked by army demands for a crackdown on religious activism.

"It was seen as suitable to go to elections in a reasonable time... The prime ministership will change hands by the end of the month," said Ciller, who had been set to take over the post under a coalition protocol signed last June.

Elections were not due until the year 2000. The call for new elections after 11 months in government with the Islamists signalled the end of another turbulent chapter in Ciller's four years in the political limelight.

Her gamble to ally with the Islamists was ultimately lost because of the secular establishment's anger over her decision last June to drag her conservative True Path Party (DYP) into a government led by her former bitter rival, Islamist leader Necmettin Erbakan.

The opposition, egged on by the military and secularist media, had accused the alliance of straying from the country's official secular order. They attacked Ciller for failing to temper the Islamist policies of Erbakan's Welfare Party.

Conservative Ciller, an astute political tactician, reversed her harsh criticism of Welfare in April 1996 after it began presenting parliament with damaging corruption charges against her dating from her time as prime minister.

She was cleared of the graft allegations that could have sent her to the Supreme Court but continued to be hounded for agreeing a power-sharing deal with Erbakan, under which she was originally to become prime minister next year.
Going into government with the Islamists flew in the face of opposition from the country's secularist elite, which U.S.-trained technocrat Ciller had often claimed to lead.

She had previously labelled Welfare leader Necmettin Erbakan, who was Turkey's first Islamist prime minister, as "the symbol of backwardness" for his plans to bring Turkey closer to the rest of the Moslem world.
The confidence of NATO-member Turkey's Western allies in Ciller's perceived pro-Western stance had also been shaken by her increasingly nationalist statements as foreign minister.

Last summer, the United States criticised her for warning that Turks would "break the hands" of anyone who insulted their flag, a reference to a Greek Cypriot who was shot dead in Cyprus while trying to tear down the Turkish flag.
She caused alarm in Western capitals in January with the threat of a military strike against missile systems the Cypriot government was planning to install on the south of the island.
"These offensive missiles will definitely not be deployed. If they are deployed we will do what is needed. If that means they need to be hit they will be hit," she told a news conference.
Further, she alienated many European Union officials with a fresh offensive aimed at winning full membership of the group.

A warning that Turkey would "not hang on as a second-rate member" of the EU was accompanied by accusations that right-wing European politicians were encouraging racist attacks against Turks in Europe through anti-Turkish prejudice.
Nevertheless, it was Ciller who took the country into a trade pact with the European Union last year that gave Turkey some of the closest ties to the union of any non-EU country.
Ciller became the first woman premier of Moslem-but-secular Turkey in 1993. Her gung-ho style has often rubbed the male-dominated, political establishment the wrong way.
She confounded her critics as she bounced from crisis to crisis in office, including a near economic meltdown, a Kurdish rebel insurgency and a host of foreign policy problems.
Ciller joined the DYP, then in opposition, in 1990 after an academic career in the United States and a spell as economics professor at Istanbul's elite Bosphorus University.
Despite her liberal credentials, Ciller was a hawk in dealing with a Kurdish separatist rebellion that began in 1984.

Her free marketeering policies and tough talk have brought comparisons with ex-British Prime Minister "Iron Lady" Margaret Thatcher, who is said to have to encouraged Ciller to run for prime minister at a dinner in London in 1993.
Ciller married businessman Ozer Ucuran, her high-school sweetheart, in 1963 and got him to take her family name -- a rare achievement for a Turkish woman. They have two sons.
